topic.title: Education: Origins and daily operation in Community Learning Centres
topic.focus: how the initiative began and how it works each day

candidate_instructions: Read all five sections. Answer Questions 1-25. Follow the stated word limits exactly.

sections.heading: A room by the harbour
sections.text: In 2012 the evening classes at the public library in Setúbal, a port city south of Lisbon, were cancelled to save money. Beatriz Correia had just retired after twenty-eight years as a primary school teacher, and three of her neighbours asked her to help them with their reading. She began by teaching four people at her kitchen table in September that year. By the following spring there were fifteen, and the local fishermen's association offered her an empty store room on Rua do Cais, where nets had once been repaired. The room gave the centre its name: Sala das Redes, or the net room. The association asks for no rent, but the centre pays the electricity bill, about 900 euros a year. Correia registered the centre as an association in 2015, mainly so that it could open a bank account in its own name.

sections.heading: How the week is arranged
sections.text: Thirteen years later the Sala das Redes teaches in two places. The net room is open on four evenings, from Monday to Thursday, and a nearby primary school, Escola da Bela Vista, has lent a classroom on Saturday mornings since 2019. There are no terms. Learners can join in any week of the year, and they attend when their work allows. Three courses run in turn: Portuguese for people who have recently arrived in the country, basic maths, and a course on using government websites, which was added in 2018 when tax forms moved onto the internet. Each session lasts ninety minutes. On a typical Tuesday evening between eighteen and twenty-five people come. Two of the teachers are paid for part-time hours; the other fourteen helpers are volunteers, and nine of them were learners at the centre first.

sections.heading: The green notebook
sections.text: Correia is now 74 and no longer teaches. She spends her Wednesday afternoons on the register, a green notebook in which every visit is written by hand. The centre keeps it for one reason: to notice who has stopped coming. If a learner is absent twice in a row, a volunteer named Nuno Salgado telephones them, usually within a week. In 2024 he made 143 such calls, and about half of the learners he spoke to came back. Nobody is turned away for arriving late, and nobody is asked why they missed a class. Correia believes this is the reason adults who left school early are willing to walk through the door at all. The system works, but it depends on people rather than paperwork, and that has begun to worry the committee.

sections.heading: Paying the bills
sections.text: The centre spends about 48,000 euros a year, and roughly two-thirds of that pays the two part-time teachers. The city council gives 18,000 euros, a private charity called the Amélia Reis Foundation gives 14,000, and the rest comes from donations and a second-hand book stall at the Saturday market. Almost all of this money is agreed twelve months at a time. The effects are practical rather than dramatic: the association cannot sign an agreement for a room that lasts longer than a year, and it cannot offer a teacher a permanent contract. One of its two teachers left in 2023 for a school job with a three-year contract. Correia calculates that she and the treasurer spend six weeks of every year writing applications for money, which is time neither of them spends with learners.

sections.heading: Questions for the future
sections.text: In 2024 the committee discussed charging for a new course in spreadsheets and simple bookkeeping, designed for people who are already in work. The fee would be small, perhaps 30 euros for six weeks, but it would be more reliable than a grant. Two members argued that any fee at all would frighten away exactly the people the centre exists to help. Others replied that a paid course could quietly pay for the free ones. No decision was taken, and the question was left until 2026. Correia is more troubled by something else. Nobody has yet agreed to take over from her, and most of what the centre knows about its learners is not written down anywhere. In March 2025 the committee agreed to look for a second coordinator to work beside her for a year.

passage.full_text:
Paragraph 1 — A room by the harbour
In 2012 the evening classes at the public library in Setúbal, a port city south of Lisbon, were cancelled to save money. Beatriz Correia had just retired after twenty-eight years as a primary school teacher, and three of her neighbours asked her to help them with their reading. She began by teaching four people at her kitchen table in September that year. By the following spring there were fifteen, and the local fishermen's association offered her an empty store room on Rua do Cais, where nets had once been repaired. The room gave the centre its name: Sala das Redes, or the net room. The association asks for no rent, but the centre pays the electricity bill, about 900 euros a year. Correia registered the centre as an association in 2015, mainly so that it could open a bank account in its own name.

Paragraph 2 — How the week is arranged
Thirteen years later the Sala das Redes teaches in two places. The net room is open on four evenings, from Monday to Thursday, and a nearby primary school, Escola da Bela Vista, has lent a classroom on Saturday mornings since 2019. There are no terms. Learners can join in any week of the year, and they attend when their work allows. Three courses run in turn: Portuguese for people who have recently arrived in the country, basic maths, and a course on using government websites, which was added in 2018 when tax forms moved onto the internet. Each session lasts ninety minutes. On a typical Tuesday evening between eighteen and twenty-five people come. Two of the teachers are paid for part-time hours; the other fourteen helpers are volunteers, and nine of them were learners at the centre first.

Paragraph 3 — The green notebook
Correia is now 74 and no longer teaches. She spends her Wednesday afternoons on the register, a green notebook in which every visit is written by hand. The centre keeps it for one reason: to notice who has stopped coming. If a learner is absent twice in a row, a volunteer named Nuno Salgado telephones them, usually within a week. In 2024 he made 143 such calls, and about half of the learners he spoke to came back. Nobody is turned away for arriving late, and nobody is asked why they missed a class. Correia believes this is the reason adults who left school early are willing to walk through the door at all. The system works, but it depends on people rather than paperwork, and that has begun to worry the committee.

Paragraph 4 — Paying the bills
The centre spends about 48,000 euros a year, and roughly two-thirds of that pays the two part-time teachers. The city council gives 18,000 euros, a private charity called the Amélia Reis Foundation gives 14,000, and the rest comes from donations and a second-hand book stall at the Saturday market. Almost all of this money is agreed twelve months at a time. The effects are practical rather than dramatic: the association cannot sign an agreement for a room that lasts longer than a year, and it cannot offer a teacher a permanent contract. One of its two teachers left in 2023 for a school job with a three-year contract. Correia calculates that she and the treasurer spend six weeks of every year writing applications for money, which is time neither of them spends with learners.

Paragraph 5 — Questions for the future
In 2024 the committee discussed charging for a new course in spreadsheets and simple bookkeeping, designed for people who are already in work. The fee would be small, perhaps 30 euros for six weeks, but it would be more reliable than a grant. Two members argued that any fee at all would frighten away exactly the people the centre exists to help. Others replied that a paid course could quietly pay for the free ones. No decision was taken, and the question was left until 2026. Correia is more troubled by something else. Nobody has yet agreed to take over from her, and most of what the centre knows about its learners is not written down anywhere. In March 2025 the committee agreed to look for a second coordinator to work beside her for a year.
